newsitem.title: UK: GOLF-SECOND WIN IN A ROW FOR LANGER.
newsitem.headline: GOLF-SECOND WIN IN A ROW FOR LANGER.

text.p: Bernhard Langer of Germany claimed his second successive European Tour title when he won the rain-hit Benson and Hedges International by two shots from Ian Woosnam of Britain on Sunday.
It was a supreme display of assured golf by Langer in the most testing of conditions which saw play suspended twice because of lightning and torrential rain.
Langer, winner of the Italian Open a week ago, posted a final round three-under par round of 69 for a 276 total. Woosnam finished with a 70 for 278.

Lee Westwood of Britain, second for much of the final round, saw his hopes perish on the 585-yard 17th. His brave but somewhat reckless attempt to reach the green with his second shot ended short and in the water and he was forced to settle for a bogey six, a 72 and a 280 total.

Ireland's Padraig Harrington finished fourth two shots further back after a 71 while Kalle Vainola, Finland's only player on the European Tour, had a 73 to finish joint fifth with Sweden's Robert Karlsson, who carded a 71.
Langer had four birdies and dropped just one shot, a tremendous feat in the swirling wind and rain.
"It has been a wonderful two weeks," he said. "It is just a matter of everything coming together at the right time. My putting's been very good and I played very well this week from tee to green.
"It was a battle against the elements and it was hard to come back out and stay focused."
Play was suspended for the second time in the day for over an hour with lightning flashing nearby hills just as the leaders were reaching the turn.
But Langer refused to join the chorus of players wanting the tournament moved back to later in the year in the hope of better weather. Last year's event was also hit by high winds and rain.
"If you think positive in these conditions it just give you a better attitude," he said. "If you moan and groan, you're going to play miserable too."
Apart from the 116,660 pounds ($189,000) prize money, victory left Langer in second place in the Ryder Cup standings.

"That's me basically confirmed in the team. It's a surprise it came so quickly. I thought it might be July or August before it happened. Now it's out of the way and I can focus on other things," he said.

Woosnam, who started the day one stroke behind Langer and level with Westwood, looked to have fallen out of contention when he turned one over par and then double-bogeyed the 10th after going into the water.
But he pulled a shot back at the next and finished in glorious style with four birdies in the last five holes.
"I'm pleased with my finish but annoyed with myself for the 10th," he said. "After the 11th I could have birdied every hole coming back."
One prime casualty of the weather was Briton Colin Montgomerie, blown out of contention for the second successive year in this tournament and who admitted he was not a good player in the wind.
His final round 81 included a triple-bogey six at the par three second hole where he needed five putts - four from three feet - to get down.
"I went back and forth. I grasp the putter lightly so that's why I've never won in a strong wind," he said.
Last year it was more painful and he stormed from the course in a rage as an overnight lead going into the final round was wrecked by an 84.
This time the European number one was never in contention. He started the last round 10 stokes behind Langer and left the 18th with a cheerful shrug of resignation.

"Never mind, I'll look forward to next week (the English Open)," he said. "But for the spectators that was no fun at all. It doesn't do us or the public any good. It's unfortunate but we say that every year.
"I personally feel the same as Seve (Ballesteros) that we shouldn't play here before July and August and play elsewhere in May."
Montgomerie said the problem was that the course was very exposed. "It's a good course, a very good course spoiled by the weather," he said.
